newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Tight supply affecting rape oil premium -trade.
newsitem.headline: Tight supply affecting rape oil premium -trade.

text.p: General tightness in the rapeseed market has left crushers short of material, and this has raised rape oil's premium over soyoil, European traders said on Thursday.
The high premium was only partly down to worries over imports of genetically modified soybeans from the U.S., traders and analysts added.

Fears that the new U.S. soybeans would prove unsellable to food processing companies in Europe -- some firms had already said they would not sell products made from the beans -- had exacerbated the trend, they said.

"There are two reasons for the premium," said Arie van Dijk of market statistician Stigevo. "The main one is the tight supplies of rapeseed and then, secondly, the psychological impact from genetically modified soybeans."
Van Dijk said a fall in this season's key German rapeseed crop -- down to an estimated 1.94 million tonnes from 3.1 million last year -- was the main reason for the tightness.
December rapeseed was trading firmly at around 470 marks a tonnes as sellers slowed down deliveries to crushers in a play that traders said was common for the time of year.

But the prospect of imports of the new beans was beginning to affect the market. Van Dijk noted an increasing number of European food firms specifying use of non-genetically altered beans. "There is definitely a trend developing," he said.
Traders said one current option for traders wishing to avoid the modified beans was to trade solely with material from Brazil and Argentina.
But some cited market speculation that 1997 plantings in Latin America would also include the new beans.
One trader reported talk that this year's crop contained "a significant amount of the new beans".
